title: URL shortener
summary: From a one-line brief to 11,458 redirects a second under 50 ms, step by step.

steps.title: Short links, fast redirects
body: Create a short code for a long URL, and send anyone who opens the code to the long URL. 100M new links a month; about 100 redirects per link created.
What matters most: a redirect is on the critical path of someone's click, so p99 must stay under 50 ms, and a link once created is never lost.

callout.text: Two numbers decide this design: reads are 100x writes, and the redirect is user-facing. Everything else follows from them.

steps.title: Put numbers on it
body: The calculator turns 3.3M creates and 330M redirects a day into a peak of about 11,458 redirects a second and 115 creates a second, with a peak multiplier of 3 (assumed).
Five years of links is 2.7 TiB, 8.2 TiB with three copies: too much for one comfortable machine, small enough for a modest cluster.

steps.title: The simplest thing that works
body: Stateless API servers behind a load balancer, and one table keyed by code. A redirect is one lookup by primary key.
Watch a request go in and the answer come back: about 38 ms at p99 on a quiet day.

steps.title: Every click lands on the store
body: At peak, all 11,458 redirects a second go to the store, and a viral link sends thousands of them to one partition.
The store runs hot, its queue grows, and the p99 climbs past the 50 ms target.

callout.text: The store is the first thing to break at today's numbers: it does the same lookup for the same hot codes thousands of times a second.

steps.title: Reads dominate: cache them
body: Put Redis in front of the store, cache-aside: check Redis, fall back to the store, then fill Redis. The hot set is at most 31 GiB, so one node and a replica hold it.
About 90% of redirects now stop at Redis in about a millisecond. Cache 'no such code' too, for 30 s, or bots asking for random codes reach the store every time.

callout.text: The cost is staleness: a taken-down link can still redirect for up to the 24 h TTL. Delete the key on takedown.

steps.decision: Redis cache-aside in front of the store

steps.title: Where do codes come from?
body: A hash of the URL, cut to 7 characters, collides after about two million links. Instead, the API takes ids from the allocator in blocks of 1,000 and encodes each in base 62.
One allocator call per 1,000 creates; no collision checks. Ids are scrambled first, so codes cannot be counted.
steps.decision: Id blocks from an allocator, base 62

steps.title: Count clicks without slowing them
body: Answer with a 302, so every click reaches us and can be counted, and a takedown works at once. The API publishes a ClickEvent and moves on; a counter consumes the stream.
This is the settled design: it is the diagram in the design doc.

steps.title: Case: the Redis node dies
body: Redis fails. All 11,458 reads a second fall through to the store; its 23-connection budget is gone in a moment and calls start timing out.
Clients retry three times, so the store sees four times the load and cannot recover on its own.

callout.text: A cache you cannot lose is a database you did not size. Plan for the cold start, not just the warm day.

steps.title: Coalesce, time out, promote
body: Three defences: one store read per hot code at a time (request coalescing), a 200 ms store timeout with a 10% retry budget, and a warm Redis replica promoted within 30 s.
The store now sees one read per distinct code while the replica takes over: busy, but inside its budget.

steps.title: At 10x: what changes first
body: At 10x the peak is about 114,583 redirects a second. The hot set outgrows one Redis node first: shard it three ways. The store adds partitions; codes hash evenly, so no partition runs hot.
At 100x, regional caches and read replicas, migrated with dual reads.

steps.title: The finished design
body: Every box earned its place with a number. The table is the doc's trade-off table: what each decision solves, what it costs, and the signal that should make you change it.
